title: The Hot Chick
full_review:
"The Hot Chick" (Touchstone) is a dumb-witted sex farce about a mean high school cheerleader who wakes up one morning in the body of a 30-something petty thief.

This happens after teen Jessica (Rachel McAdams) drops -- and crook Clive (Rob Schneider) finds -- a magical earring which she has stolen from an African shopkeeper to wear at her prom.

Confusion reigns among family and friends as Jessica tries to hide her misfortune through various pretenses while carrying on as teen queen-bee, daughter and girlfriend, until she can track down her lost earring and resume her normal life.

Co-writer Schneider and director-co-writer Tom Brady prefer crude toilet humor, witless sex jokes, racial slurs and sophomoric cliches about true love to anything resembling a good comedy of errors.

Cheerleader Jessica, rich and spoiled by her parents, and her clique of girlfriends cruise in her shiny new car, flirting with the football jocks. In a series of encounters with various classmates, servants and assorted workers, Jessica humiliates them as if they are scum put on the earth only for her amusement and abuse.

One of these grubs is Clive, who is in the midst of robbing a gas station just as the girls pull in for a fill-up. Clive poses as the filling station attendant, gets his share of abuse and, as the girls drive off, finds one of Jessica's earrings dropped on the pavement. Another jewel in his bag of loot, he takes the earring.

The morning after Clive puts on the earring, Jessica wakes up in Clive's body, and Clive in Jessica's.

What follows is a series of loosely connected comic bits as Jessica tries to convince her girlfriends what has happened and that she is really Jessica underneath a male exterior. To blend in with her family, Jessica poses as a Mexican house gardener, but the portrayal is stereotypical and racist. It becomes tasteless as Jessica in this guise gets to hear her father talk about his sex life with her mother.

To fit in at school, Schneider's character poses as a janitor who frequents the jocks' locker room making sexually suggestive remarks in scenes laced with homophobic double entendres. Around girlfriends' homes, Schneider cross-dresses in the most absurd and skimpy drag. His idea of how to portray a girl is to think of the most flamboyant, prancing homosexual stereotype and then imitate it.

One stupefying slur at the expense of Catholics involves Jessica calling a boy and, in a man's voice, saying, "I should have made love to you when I had the chance." The boyfriend replies, "Father Mulcahy?"

Through these subterfuges, Jessica learns that she is not well-liked at all and that her boyfriend and his friends are all two-timing cheats.

Jessica spends the rest of the movie wooing her boyfriend (fodder for more homosexual entendres), making amends with those she's humiliated, and avenging her cheated-upon girlfriends. When she's accomplished all of the above, her life gets to revert to normal. But first she has to convince her best friend not to have a lesbian encounter with her at the school prom.

Now, hopefully, no one needs to be convinced that this dreadful movie is worth seeing.

Due to a benign view of teen promiscuity, brief violence, drug references, racial and anti-Catholic slurs, homosexual activity and innuendo, brief rear nudity, gross body-fluid humor and constant crude language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
